topic.description: Lake Powell falls to its lowest level on record after a dry, warm winter (Sep 2026).

news.title: New map highlights which US rivers should be priorities for protection
news.text:
A new map has revealed which American rivers need the most attention and protection amid the worsening climate crisis.

Only six percent of these water bodies are currently in good condition and 14 percent need help, con-servationists and scientists said in a September study.

That’s because a century of changes to the landscape and groundwater usage have forced species that live in rivers into a rapid decline.

But by identifying these areas, the researchers say there’s already been progress to protect the rivers. Dams have been identified for removal and land has been prioritized for protection around the rivers’ sources.

“We can now point at a map for the first time and say, these are the rivers most capable of sustaining diversity of aquatic life, and this is what each one needs,” Mary Khoury, a freshwater ecologist at The Nature Conservancy, which led the study, told Science News on Wednesday.

The four-year-long analysis - which included 5.2 million miles of rivers and streams in the lower 48 - showed that a third were above-average for resilience to manmade climate change. Although these rivers may still require restoration.

These rivers are found along the Pacific Coast, the Northern Rocky Mountains, the Great Lakes areas in Wisconsin and Minnesota, in Northern Maine and in coastal regions along the southeastern U.S. and the Gulf Coast.

Vulnerable or below-average resilience river networks made up 15 percent. These were located in the Southwest deserts, lower New England, the shortgrass prairie east of the Rocky Mountains and the agricultural lands of the Midwestern states.

The rivers and their surrounding areas were rated on how connected the river network is, whether animals can freely travel through them, water quality and the condition of the land near the river, how much water it is, and how much its flows have been altered.

“A resilient system is one that gives species options and environments in which to adapt,” Khoury noted.

The team acknowledged that the maps don’t take human needs into account, but said data representing human dimensions could be combined with this analysis to identify them.

Climate change has degraded water quality in U.S. rivers due to flooding, fires, sea level rise, droughts, changes to groundwater and many other impacts, according to the non-profit National Environmental Education Foundation.

Rising temperatures can create toxic algal blooms that harm river ecosystems and lead to the spread of disease. 

Historic heat has helped Lake Mead and Lake Powell - two of America’s largest reservoirs - reach record low levels this summer. The Southwest reservoirs are offshoots of the shrinking Colorado River.

Three-quarters of rivers could lose their biodiversity due to climate change, the Nature Conservancy said in a release accompanying the research.
news.summary: Three-quarters of rivers could lose their biodiversity due to climate change, conservationists say
news.author: Julia Musto

news.title: Satellite Images Show How Lake Powell Has Drained to Record Low in 9 Years
news.text: Newly released satellite images show the startling retreat of Lake Powell over nine years. They compare the lake near Glen Canyon Dam on September 1, 2017, with the same area on September 10, 2026, and come after prolonged drought contributed to the reservoir reaching its lowest recorded level. NASA described the reservoir’s 2017 level as one of its highest of the preceding decade. The second image, captured on September 10, 2026, showed substantially less water in the reservoir. The agency said the 2026 image was captured as Lake Powell’s water level stood at 3,517.24 feet—roughly a month after its levels fell below the previous record low of 3,519.92 feet, which was set in April 2023. Why Lake Powell and the Colorado River System Matter Lake Powell, the second-largest reservoir in the U.S., sits along the drought-stricken Colorado River, which runs approximately 1,400 miles and supports seven states—Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah and Wyoming—as well as Mexico. The river provides municipal water for tens of millions while supporting hydropower, recreation, fish and wildlife, as well as millions of acres of agricultural land. Major Colorado River Reservoirs Reached Record Lows NASA’s release of the images comes after both Lake Powell and Lake Mead—the largest reservoir in the U.S.—hit record lows in August. The Bureau of Reclamation, which manages both reservoirs, said the new lows followed a record-low winter snowpack in the Colorado River Basin in 2025-2026. Mead’s record low was “discouraging but not surprising," Sarah Porter, director of the Kyl Center for Water Policy at Arizona State University, told Newsweek previously. "The reservoir will likely recover at least a little this winter, and with very heavy snowpack it could recover a lot, but levels at both Lake Mead and Lake Powell have ratcheted down over the last quarter century and one good winter won’t be enough to stabilize the system over the long term." In April, federal water managers announced actions intended to help bolster falling water levels in Lake Powell, including the release of water from upstream Flaming Gorge Reservoir and a reduction in releases from Lake Powell downstream to Lake Mead. The Bureau of Reclamation had warned that “without major intervention,” water level decline in Lake Powell could threaten hydropower production at Glen Canyon Dam. Lake Powell Levels Could Rise in Coming Years New federal projections released earlier this week indicated that Lake Powell’s level could rise by some 40 feet over the next two years, though the same projection suggested Lake Mead’s could fall by a similar amount. The Bureau of Reclamation’s September 2026 “most probable” 24-Month Study, under a scenario in which 6 million acre-feet of water is released from Lake Powell in the 2027 operating year, showed Lake Powell rising to 3,558.44 feet by June 2028. Lake Mead, on the other hand, could fall to 998.40 feet in August that year, according to the projections. Contact Newsweek editor on this story: Edward Pearcey.
news.summary: Images published by NASA show the major reservoir's decline, after the lake hit a record low in August.
news.author: Joe Edwards

news.title: Lake Mead Water Levels Projected to Sharply Drop as Lake Powell Benefits
news.text: New federal projections for the Colorado River’s two largest reservoirs indicate that Lake Mead’s water level could fall by around 40 feet over the next two years while Lake Powell’s rises by a similar amount. The Bureau of Reclamation’s September 2026 “most probable” 24-Month Study, under a scenario in which 6 million acre-feet of water is released from Lake Powell in the 2027 operating year, suggests both reservoirs could see notable water level changes. These studies are updated monthly to support Colorado River operations and planning. Under this scenario, Lake Mead is forecast to fall to an elevation of 1,007.38 by July 2027. Its level is then projected to rise to 1,020.51 by February 2028, before declining to 998.40 feet in August that year. Lake Powell, by contrast, could rise to 3,542 feet in June 2027. After falling in March 2028 to 3,518.08 feet, it is projected to rise to 3,558.44 feet by June 2028. Newsweek contacted the Bureau of Reclamation for comment via email. Why the Colorado River System Matters The Colorado River runs approximately 1,400 miles, supporting seven states—Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah and Wyoming—as well as parts of Mexico. Tens of millions rely on the river's resources for at least some municipal water, and it also supports hydropower, recreation, fish and wildlife, and millions of acres of agricultural land. Lakes Mead and Powell Reached Record Lows The latest Bureau of Reclamation projections show both reservoirs reaching record lows in August. The agency said the record-low elevations followed a record-low winter snowpack in the Colorado River Basin in 2025-2026. It also said their combined storage was lower than at any point since before Lake Powell began filling in 1963. The record low at Lake Mead was “discouraging but not surprising," Sarah Porter, director of the Kyl Center for Water Policy at Arizona State University, told Newsweek previously. "The reservoir will likely recover at least a little this winter, and with very heavy snowpack it could recover a lot, but levels at both Lake Mead and Lake Powell have ratcheted down over the last quarter century and one good winter won’t be enough to stabilize the system over the long term." As of Tuesday, Lake Powell’s elevation was around 3516.62, according to data compiled by the U.S. Lakes monitoring website. Lake Mead’s elevation was 1038.51 as of Thursday. April Actions Added Water to Lake Powell In April, the Bureau of Reclamation announced measures to protect Lake Powell and infrastructure at Glen Canyon Dam after projections indicated the lake could drop to levels that threatened hydropower generation without major intervention. “If Glen Canyon Dam declines below 3,490 feet, water releases would be only through the river outlet works, which could cause operational issues, uncertainty for users, downstream impacts, instability in regional power and water supplies, and a reduction in power generation,” the agency warned at the time. It said it intended to add up to about 2.48 million acre-feet to Powell through two actions. Firstly, between 660,000 acre-feet and 1 million acre-feet would be released from Flaming Gorge Reservoir between April 2026 and April 2027. The Bureau of Reclamation also said it would reduce the annual volume scheduled to pass from Lake Powell through Glen Canyon Dam toward Lake Mead by 1.48 million acre-feet, lowering it from 7.48 million to 6 million acre-feet through September 2026. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: John Fitzpatrick and Sam Wilson.
news.summary: Federal water managers released new projections for the U.S.'s two largest reservoirs this week.
news.author: Joe Edwards

news.title: Why El Niño Monsoons Won't Provide Cure To Lake Mead Water Crisis
news.text: Monsoon rainfall is expected to hit parts of the drought-stricken Southwest this week, bringing some risk of flash flooding but offering little help to the depleted Colorado River system. While the moisture could provide localized, short-term drought relief, meteorologists say it will not deliver the prolonged rain and mountain snow needed to substantially improve conditions at Lake Mead and other major reservoirs. "Don’t expect much help at all for the Colorado River Basin," Alex Wallace, on-camera meteorologist at The Weather Channel, told Newsweek. "There may be some areas that pick up a couple of inches of rain over the next few days but to truly get back to normal, they need a lot more." In an email sent to Newsweek on Tuesday, AccuWeather said its meteorologists forecast moderate rainfall across the region through Friday, with the heaviest precipitation expected in Western and Northern New Mexico, eastern Arizona and Southwestern Colorado. The company said a "surge" of tropical moisture is likely to bring repeated rounds of showers and thunderstorms to the Southwest, which could provide drought relief but also raise the risk of flash flooding in areas. AccuWeather said the pattern is associated with the seasonal monsoon, historically influenced by El Niño, while noting that the strength of the North American Monsoon is also shaped by upper-level high pressure patterns and the transport of atmospheric moisture. On Wednesday, AccuWeather said rainfall of 1 to 2 inches is forecast through Thursday across the interior Southwest. Much of Central and Eastern Arizona, including Phoenix and Tucson, could see 2 to 4 inches. AccuWeather cautioned, however, that while the expected rainfall may offer some short-term relief in parts of the drought-affected Colorado River Basin, it is unlikely to make up for years of drought and water shortages. "This region has been suffering from a multi-decadal drought since the mid-1990s. It's long-term, and that is why the Colorado Basin's rivers and reservoirs are near record lows," AccuWeather lead long-range expert Paul Pastelok said in the Tuesday email. Lake Mead dropped to approximately 1,040 feet in August 2026, surpassing previous low marks from the 2022 drought. "Over time, we continue to see the rollover impacts each year and river levels just get worse. The region needs prolonged stretches of rain and snow over several years during the winter to really reverse the trend." Why the Colorado River Matters The Colorado River is about 1,400 miles long and its basin covers approximately 250,000 square miles. The river supports water supplies, hydropower, recreation and wildlife habitat across seven U.S. states and Mexico. According to the Bureau of Reclamation, some 40 million people rely on the river for municipal water, and it sustains 5.5 million acres of farmland. The agency also says the river’s hydroelectric facilities produce more than 8 billion kilowatt-hours annually, enough to meet the needs of approximately 700,000 homes. Lakes Mead and Powell—the first- and second-largest reservoirs in the U.S., respectively—both plummeted to record lows in August following what federal water managers described as prolonged drought and the lowest snowpack on record. "The monsoon has certainly provided the Southwest the bulk share of the rain they will see for the year but when you look at the numbers, it has essentially been an average, if not slightly below average, season of rainfall," said Wallace. "Since the onset of the monsoon, there hasn’t been a substantial change in the drought situation across the Southwest. "The rain expected for the remainder of this week will be beneficial and there will be some local improvement to the drought. However, overall, I wouldn’t expect to see whole category changes in the amount of drought in the region." Wallace added that meaningful long-term drought relief would likely require multiple years of favorable conditions, including wet monsoon seasons and snowy winters. The meteorologist noted that strong snowpack is especially important because melting snow ultimately feeds water into the Colorado River Basin. "The bottom line is that if we are looking for some long-term drought relief, we should be hoping for winters filled with snow piling up," said Wallace. As the current Colorado River operating rules expire at the end of 2026, negotiations and federal decisions over a post-2026 framework will determine how water shortages and reservoir operations are managed amid continuing drought and declining river flows. The seven basin states remain divided over how the shrinking river supply and future cutbacks should be shared between the Upper and Lower Basins, with no consensus framework reached. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Matthew Robinson and James Debens
news.summary: “Don’t expect much help at all for the Colorado River Basin,” one meteorologist told Newsweek.
news.author: Joe Edwards

news.title: A Drought, the Colorado River, and the Hoover Dam
news.text:
BOULDER CITY, Nev.—At Lake Mead’s Callville Bay Marina, exposed-rock bluffs now rise above the shoreline where the lake once covered the land.

A brown-and-white sign marks a vanished 2000 shoreline—and the beginning of a decades-long regional megadrought.

Farther downslope, the marina and boat slips come into view, but reaching them on foot requires a hike through 100-degree heat.

The drought has transformed the man-made lake into a shrunken version of itself, with no end in sight. The falling water level threatens supplies and hydroelectric power for millions and has forced some boat ramps to close.

“It’s getting pretty scary. You know, the water’s dropping to a level where they can’t keep up with marking the hazards,” a marina employee told The Epoch Times, requesting anonymity.

“It’s hard for people to launch their boats because the water level is dropping at such a pace. The maintenance to keep up the launch ramps is difficult.”

In some cases, shallow water has left boaters with broken propellers and scraped hulls after they’ve struck rocks and debris that were once deep underwater.

The employee pointed toward a location hundreds of feet away.

“Can you see the cement over there?”

That’s where the water once lapped against the shoreline, the employee said.

Now, green grass grows along the dry lake bottom.

“You can see the years and the levels where the water was. It just keeps going down and down and down,” the employee said.

“Look around. I mean, this is serious. Look how quiet it is.”

But Lake Mead is only part of the story. Its fate is tied to Lake Powell, its sister reservoir about 300 miles upstream, and ultimately to the Colorado River that supplies them both.

Warmer temperatures and declining snowpack have reduced the water feeding the river and, by extension, the lakes. All are critical sources of power for dams that provide hydroelectric power for customers across the Southwest.

Olivia Conner, a land shuttle driver at Calville Marina, said she’s witnessed severe droughts before, but nothing like the regional drought of the past two decades.

“There has been a huge drop in the lake levels this year for sure. It’s about at the lowest point it’s ever been right now,” Conner told The Epoch Times.

Hydroelectric reservoirs have two critical thresholds. “Dead pool” marks the point at which water can no longer move downstream by gravity. “Power pool” is the minimum level needed for water to reach the intakes that feed the dams’ hydroelectric turbines.

Lake Mead is currently at 1,039 feet above mean sea level and 26 percent full, down from its 1,229-foot full pool, and 18 feet lower than in 2025. The reservoir is currently at 144 feet above dead pool and 89 feet above power pool.

When it reaches dead pool, it will be unable to power the Hoover Dam. The massive dam, built in 1931, supplies the power needs of nearly 8 million people.

Lake Powell, the nation’s second-largest reservoir behind Lake Mead, is just under 22 percent full, about 183 feet below its 3,700-foot full pool and roughly 29 feet lower than a year ago.

The reservoir supplies water to Glen Canyon Dam, which supplies electricity to roughly 5 million customers. At the current drought level, the reservoir sits 147 feet above dead pool and 27 feet above power pool.

The Colorado River runs 1,400 miles from the Continental Divide in Colorado to the Gulf of California in Mexico.

Its basin spans 250,000 square miles and is a critical resource for the seven states it crosses, according to the Bureau of Reclamation, which oversees the reservoirs and dams at both lakes.

Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah, and Wyoming depend on the river for water, hydropower, recreation, and natural habitat.

“Although agricultural uses depend on 70 percent of Colorado water, between 35 [million] and 40 million people rely on the same water for some, if not all, of their municipal needs,” the Bureau of Reclamation states.

Some of the river’s water also flows to Mexico under a 1944 treaty, the agency adds.

More than 5 million acres of farmland and 30 tribal nations draw water from the river and its tributaries.

Situated in the downstream, lower portion of the Colorado River basin, Lower Basin states are allocated 7.5 million acre-feet annually under the 1922 Colorado River Compact. California, with senior water rights, claims 4.4 million acre-feet; Arizona, 2.8 million; and Nevada, 300,000.

Since the Colorado River megadrought began at the turn of the millennium, Lower Basin states have watched their water evaporate into thin air.

Evaporation accounted for 61 percent of the drought’s severity between 2020 and 2022, as shown in National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration research. Less rainfall accounted for the remaining 39 percent.

Droughts can develop even when precipitation remains within a normal range, as higher temperatures and evaporation remove water from soils, the organization said.

Even modest warming can make droughts longer, broader, and more severe.

Reservoirs in the Upper Basin states are faring better. Wyoming’s Flaming Gorge is 71 percent full; western Colorado’s Crystal Creek Reservoir is at 89 percent; and the state’s Morrow Point reservoir is at 97 percent, the Central Arizona Project says.

On Aug. 21, the Department of the Interior issued new operating guidelines for 2027–2028, requiring the Lower Basin states to reduce Colorado River water use by 1.25 million acre-feet annually.

That includes 760,000 acre-feet from Arizona, 440,000 from California, and 50,000 from Nevada. The states must also voluntarily conserve and store an additional 700,000 acre-feet over two years.

No mandatory restrictions are required for Upper Basin states—Colorado, New Mexico, Utah, and Wyoming—under the new guidelines.

The guidelines establish a 10-year framework for managing the Colorado River and protecting critical infrastructure at Glen Canyon and Hoover dams.

They also provide flexible tools and voluntary conservation measures to address the prolonged drought, the department said.

The Interior Department added that since January 2025, the Trump administration has invested more than $3 billion in water delivery, storage, distribution, treatment, and efficiency projects across the Colorado River Basin.

Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs praised the plan.

“With this plan, we saved Arizona from forced federal cuts that would have crippled our economy and America’s national security,” Hobbs said in a statement.

However, she criticized what she described as unequal treatment of Lower and Upper Basin states.

“The federal decision also protects Upper Basin reservoirs at the expense of Lake Mead and falls short of providing the water that the Lower Basin is entitled to, all while the threat of unilateral federal cutbacks in future years remains,” she said.

Colorado Gov. Jared Polis said Upper Basin states were “encouraged” by guidelines that will “better reflect existing water supply, which must underpin any practicable plan going forward.”

“The water supply realities of the Basin cannot be ignored or papered over,” Polis said in a statement. “States in both the Upper and Lower divisions of the basin are feeling the pain of severe drought.

“This is a reality that all states, and the federal government, will need to address practically, which is why a seven-state agreement will provide the best outcome for all water users in the Colorado River Basin.”

At Lake Powell in Page, Arizona—population 7,440—receding shorelines are affecting access to more than drinking water.

The main concern is infrastructure for launching and retrieving boats, said city public information officer Adam Geller.

Declining water levels have also hurt local revenues.

Since June 2025, the city’s sales tax revenue was down more than 11 percent and hotel tax revenue fell more than 22 percent, Geller said.

Short-term rental occupancy is down 10 percent. Hotel occupancy fell roughly 6 percent in July.

“We saw similar declines for May and June as well,” Geller told The Epoch Times.

The decline is largely tied to boating and multiday visits, he said.

Horseshoe Bend and nearby Antelope Canyon, the city’s two biggest attractions, are less affected by lake levels and continue to draw visitors.

Both, however, have seen some declines due to factors including slower international tourism and higher fuel costs.

The National Park Service manages lake ramps. It has funding for projects at Antelope Point, Bullfrog Marina, and other locations that will extend ramp access to cope with low water elevation.

“On our end, we’re working to promote tourism and improve the experience people have when they get here,” he said.

Plans include downtown beautification, new trails, digital passports to encourage longer stays, and promoting Page as the hub of the Grand Circle—the road trip loop that includes the Grand Canyon and several other national parks and monuments across the Southwest.

The city has also approved land sales for two new luxury resorts. Retail and restaurant developments are also planned, Geller said.

Geller said the city is planning around a “realistic possibility” that reduced lake access could continue and affect local businesses.

The Department of the Interior’s new operating guidelines set 3,510 feet as a protective target for the lake, with releases managed to defend that level, he said.

“Current federal projections still show the lake dipping below 3,510 in the coming water year, so we’re not overselling the near term. But having a defended long-term floor is real progress,” Geller said.

Protecting Page’s economy and quality of life will require “honest, realistic planning,” Geller added.

“That means telling people plainly what lake access looks like right now, continuing to build the kind of experience that keeps visitors here longer regardless of lake level, and staying engaged with the federal agencies who control the timeline for any of this to turn around,” he said.

Mikayla Daw, manager of Stix Liquor and Sporting Goods in Page, said Lake Powell’s declining level hasn’t yet been a major concern. There has still been plenty of water for sailing and fishing.

“But now it’s just getting lower and lower,” she told The Epoch Times. “It wasn’t busy this summer, it was just pretty much a little bit lower than what you would expect.

“As far as business, we’re doing pretty good. We’re keeping it steady.”

The falling water has also created new recreational opportunities, including hiking along newly exposed areas, she said.

On a recent August morning, Antelope Marina was still serving tourists with boat and Sea-Doo rentals, lake tours, and a restaurant.

“The lake is still there. There’s stuff to do on the lake,” Daw said. She believes higher gas and diesel prices have had more of a negative impact than dropping water levels.

“So the best thing to do is just kind of promote things and tell everybody the lake is still here.

“Everybody kind of thinks fall season is going to be an all-time low, but I’m keeping it positive.”

Lacee Nichols, a boat driver at Lake Powell Paddle Boards and Kayaks in Page, said the man-made lake appears to be at its lowest level since 1963, when it was formed.

“We’re not having to carry our kayaks up and down a very long hill now that it’s dropped so much,” Nichols told The Epoch Times.

“There have been quite a few more rocks and cliffs coming up out of the water, so it’s just making sure we pay attention.”

Despite the prolonged drought and lower water levels, life on the lake continues much as before, she said.

“You can still do about the same activities out here that you used to,“ Nichols said. ”Personally, I would love our water to come back. It keeps customers from worrying so much.”

At Lake Mead, Conner also stays positive. “The problem is just at the shorelines,“ she said. ”Once you get out there on Lake Mead, it’s still beautiful. There’s still tons of water, plenty of space to recreate.”

Conner is hoping that predictions of an increasingly strong El Niño later in 2026 will bring more rain—and much-needed relief.

“We are hoping for the best,” she said.
news.author: Allan Stein

Plans include downtown beautification, new trails, digital passports to encourage longer stays, and promoting Page as the hub of the Grand Circle—the road trip loop that includes the Grand Canyon and several other national parks and monuments across the Southwest.

The city has also approved land sales for two new luxury resorts. Retail and restaurant developments are also planned, Geller said.

Geller said the city is planning around a “realistic possibility” that reduced lake access could continue and affect local businesses.

The Department of the Interior’s new operating guidelines set 3,510 feet as a protective target for the lake, with releases managed to defend that level, he said.

“Current federal projections still show the lake dipping below 3,510 in the coming water year, so we’re not overselling the near term. But having a defended long-term floor is real progress,” Geller said.

Protecting Page’s economy and quality of life will require “honest, realistic planning,” Geller added.

“That means telling people plainly what lake access looks like right now, continuing to build the kind of experience that keeps visitors here longer regardless of lake level, and staying engaged with the federal agencies who control the timeline for any of this to turn around,” he said.

Mikayla Daw, manager of Stix Liquor and Sporting Goods in Page, said Lake Powell’s declining level hasn’t yet been a major concern. There has still been plenty of water for sailing and fishing.

“But now it’s just getting lower and lower,” she told The Epoch Times. “It wasn’t busy this summer, it was just pretty much a little bit lower than what you would expect.

“As far as business, we’re doing pretty good. We’re keeping it steady.”

The falling water has also created new recreational opportunities, including hiking along newly exposed areas, she said.

On a recent August morning, Antelope Marina was still serving tourists with boat and Sea-Doo rentals, lake tours, and a restaurant.

“The lake is still there. There’s stuff to do on the lake,” Daw said. She believes higher gas and diesel prices have had more of a negative impact than dropping water levels.

“So the best thing to do is just kind of promote things and tell everybody the lake is still here.

“Everybody kind of thinks fall season is going to be an all-time low, but I’m keeping it positive.”

Lacee Nichols, a boat driver at Lake Powell Paddle Boards and Kayaks in Page, said the man-made lake appears to be at its lowest level since 1963, when it was formed.

“We’re not having to carry our kayaks up and down a very long hill now that it’s dropped so much,” Nichols told The Epoch Times.

“There have been quite a few more rocks and cliffs coming up out of the water, so it’s just making sure we pay attention.”

Despite the prolonged drought and lower water levels, life on the lake continues much as before, she said.

“You can still do about the same activities out here that you used to,“ Nichols said. ”Personally, I would love our water to come back. It keeps customers from worrying so much.”

At Lake Mead, Conner also stays positive. “The problem is just at the shorelines,“ she said. ”Once you get out there on Lake Mead, it’s still beautiful. There’s still tons of water, plenty of space to recreate.”

Conner is hoping that predictions of an increasingly strong El Niño later in 2026 will bring more rain—and much-needed relief.

“We are hoping for the best,” she said.
news.summary: Falling levels threaten water supplies and hydroelectric power for millions.
news.author: Allan Stein

news.title: Lake Mead Water Level Update After Hitting Record Low From Drought
news.text: Lake Mead's dramatic decline appears to be slowing, offering a small measure of relief after the reservoir fell to record-low levels during another punishing summer for the Colorado River system. As of Thursday morning, Lake Mead stood at 1,038.83 feet above sea level, according to water-level data compiled by the U.S. Lakes monitoring website, leaving the nation's largest reservoir roughly 190 feet below its full-pool elevation. The latest readings show the lake hovering near the same level it occupied in recent days, a sign that the rapid seasonal drawdown that characterized much of the spring and summer is beginning to level off. The slowdown comes after a year in which Lake Mead pushed beyond previous historic lows amid ongoing drought, weak runoff and long-term strain on the Colorado River basin. Federal projections released earlier this summer indicated the reservoir could continue falling through the end of the year, although the pace of decline has recently eased. Newsweek reached out to the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, which manages Lake Mead, by email for comment and is awaiting a response. The apparent stabilization is noteworthy because it follows a seasonal pattern that water managers have observed for years, although this year's timeline looks somewhat delayed. Typically, Lake Mead experiences its steepest declines during the spring and early summer as downstream water demand rises and reservoir releases continue. In many recent years, the rate of decline has begun to taper off around July before water levels flatten and gradually start climbing during August and September. The gains often become more noticeable later in the water year as winter storms build mountain snowpack across the Colorado River watershed and spring runoff begins flowing back into the system. This year, however, the lake continued falling deeper into the summer than is often seen. Historical readings on the U.S. Lakes archive show that while water levels are now hovering near 1,039 feet, the descent continued through much of August before showing signs of leveling out in recent weeks. The slowdown does not mean a recovery is underway. Instead, it suggests the reservoir may be transitioning from its period of rapid seasonal losses into the flatter portion of its annual cycle. The broader context remains sobering. Earlier this year, Lake Mead slipped below levels reached during the historic 2022 water crisis, marking the lowest elevation recorded since the reservoir was filled nearly 90 years ago. The milestone underscored the severity of the long-running drought and the growing imbalance between water supply and demand across the Colorado River Basin. The Colorado River supports water deliveries for tens of millions of people across the American West, while also providing irrigation supplies, hydropower generation and environmental benefits. Researchers have warned that both Lake Mead and upstream Lake Powell remain under significant pressure despite periodic wet years. Even if Lake Mead begins inching upward over the coming months, experts have repeatedly cautioned that a single wet season is unlikely to restore the reservoir to anything close to the levels seen several decades ago. The problem extends beyond one dry year. Scientists describe the basin's challenges as the product of more than two decades of drought, warming temperatures and persistent overuse of water resources. In addition, higher temperatures increase evaporation and reduce the amount of runoff that ultimately reaches reservoirs. While particularly snowy winters can temporarily boost reservoir elevations, they do not erase the broader deficit that has accumulated over decades. "We are never going to see a year where this [problem] magically goes away," weather and climate scientist Daniel Swain previously told Newsweek. "We could have the wettest year on record in the basin, and we would still have a major water deficit in the long run." As a result, even a modest rebound during the coming water year would likely represent a short-term improvement rather than a complete reversal of the reservoir's troubles. Could El Niño Help This Winter? One factor receiving increased attention is the potential development of a very strong El Niño. El Niño refers to a periodic warming of waters in the tropical Pacific Ocean that can alter weather patterns around the globe. Historically, stronger El Niño events have often increased the likelihood of wetter conditions across parts of the Southwest, though the exact impacts vary from year to year. Swain said that a strong El Niño could increase snowpack across portions of the Colorado River watershed and potentially provide a meaningful boost to Lake Mead's water levels next year. He noted that such a pattern could produce a "significant jump" in reservoir levels compared with what would otherwise be expected. Still, even favorable winter weather would not solve the basin's longer-term challenges. Swain and other experts have emphasized that the Colorado River system faces structural water shortages driven by both climate conditions and demand that exceeds the river's long-term supply. For now, the latest data suggest that Lake Mead's historic plunge may finally be slowing. Whether that stabilization evolves into a meaningful rebound will depend largely on what happens during the upcoming winter snow season, which remains the single most important source of water for the Colorado River system. What Happens Next Lake Mead's water level will continue to fluctuate in the coming weeks as federal managers balance inflows from the Colorado River with downstream water deliveries and hydropower operations at Hoover Dam. The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation updates its short-term outlooks regularly and also publishes longer-range projections that help determine potential water shortage declarations and operating conditions for the river system. While Lake Mead remains well below its historic highs, future levels will depend heavily on snowpack, runoff and precipitation across the Colorado River Basin in the months ahead. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Anna Skinner and James Debens
news.summary: Federal projections released earlier this summer indicated the reservoir could continue falling through the end of the year.
news.author: Anna Skinner
